The Banded bullfrog (Kaloula pulchra) exhibits a life history finely tuned to the ephemeral water bodies it inhabits across Southeast Asia. Egg fertilisation occurs within foam nests deposited at the water's surface following amplexus, with the resulting melanised eggs hatching after a brief incubation. Under a constant thermal regime of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the embryonic period lasts approximately 15 days [ab = approximately 15 days], after which the endotrophic larvae emerge. These yolk-sac larvae are remarkably small, with a wet weight at birth of just 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter of 1.5 mm. This diminutive size at hatching reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the developing embryo and sets the stage for a rapid larval growth phase before the onset of filter feeding on suspended algae.

The free-swimming tadpoles progress through a series of Gosner stages while feeding actively on plankton and periphyton in warm, rain-filled pools. At a water temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the larval development from hatching to the onset of metamorphosis spans approximately 45 days . This relatively rapid transformation is characteristic of species breeding in temporary habitats, allowing individuals to escape drying ponds before the aquatic environment disappears. During this period, the tadpoles undergo substantial morphological transformation, including limb bud development and tail resorption, culminating in the emergence of tiny froglets that begin their terrestrial existence. The timing of this critical transition is tightly linked to the stability of the aquatic habitat.

Following metamorphosis, the juvenile froglets embark on a period of somatic growth that continues until the attainment of sexual maturity, which occurs at 547 days following metamorphosis [tp = 547 days following metamorphosis] when maintained at 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This extended juvenile phase, lasting nearly one and a half years, allows the individuals to reach a body size sufficient to support the energetic demands of reproduction. Female Banded bullfrogs ultimately achieve an asymptotic body mass of approximately 120 grams [Wwi = approximately 120 grams], a value representing the upper end of the reported range for the species and reflecting the substantial investment in both body maintenance and future gamete production.

The species displays a maximum lifespan of approximately 11 years [am = approximately 11 years] when kept under stable laboratory conditions at 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This extended longevity, exceeding that of many similarly sized anurans, is likely linked to their fossorial habits during dry periods, which reduces exposure to predators and harsh environmental conditions. The basal oxygen consumption of adult Banded bullfrogs measured at rest is 0.0134 milliliters per hour [JOi = 0.0134 milliliters per hour] at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], demonstrating a modest metabolic rate that may be an adaptation to their relatively sedentary, ambush-feeding lifestyle and periodic estivation.

Reproductive output in this species is substantial, with females typically producing a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year] during the monsoon season. Each clutch contains approximately 5000 to 7500 eggs [N_R_i = Each clutch contains approximately 5000 to 7500 eggs], which together yields an approximate annual reproductive output of 5000 eggs per year under optimal conditions at 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This high fecundity is consistent with an r-selected strategy adapted to unpredictable aquatic habitats where larval survival is highly stochastic. The gravid female, capable of carrying such large clutches due to her 120 gram adult mass, invests heavily in a single explosive breeding event each year, capitalizing on the brief window of habitat availability.
